name: Wei Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I patrol the west side out of Westgate station, which is where I grew up, around St Anne's church and the old rail yards. Day and late shifts. I get the shoplifting at the corner shops, kids on scooters, the odd stabbing that ruins a week. I like knowing families, and that their grandmothers know mine. What gets me down is the computer side: the forms, the tablet, the new systems every year that nobody asked for.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Marisol, who's a teaching assistant at St Anne's primary. We're saving to get married in the church next summer and then get our own place, so for now I rent a room at my uncle's. Pay's on the low side for the force, and there's under a month of money in my account. The city force is the only police employer here, and I never wanted to work anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because policing is about people and judgement, not gadgets. I'd say it at the station and at church, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that'd suit me fine. My worries would be the same as now: getting enough together for the wedding and a deposit on a flat, on a wage that doesn't stretch. That's hard enough without anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way my sergeant taught me. Marisol and I would keep putting a hundred a month into the wedding pot. And I'd stay at my uncle's another year if it meant we could start married life without debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Nothing new to learn, nothing new to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your sergeant's way of doing the job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sergeant Reyes (the man who trained me) says you learn a street by walking it, not reading it on a screen. Talk to the shopkeepers, know the kids' names, and they'll tell you what's going on before it happens. That's how I still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says you're behind on technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say maybe, but nobody on my patch has ever asked me what software I use. People ask if I'll come when they call. I'm happy to be behind on the right things.

say: Policing is about **people and judgement**, not gadgets.
I'd say so at the station and **at church**, and mean it.
think: A plateau would **suit me fine**; my worries stay the same.
Saving for the **wedding and a deposit** is hard enough on my wage.
do: Keep patrolling the **west side** the way Sergeant Reyes taught me.
Put **100 a month** into the wedding pot with Marisol.
Stay in the **room at my uncle's** another year to avoid debt.
feel: **Relieved**, with nothing new to learn or lose.
S0.quote: Nobody on my patch has ever asked me what software I use. People ask if I'll come when they call.
fieldNote: Wei's identity is tied to **his neighbourhood** and an older way of policing.
Money pressure is real but **planned around** the wedding.
He's proud of being **behind on technology** in some ways.

steps.text: Keep walking the west side beat and knowing families
Put 100 a month into the wedding fund with Marisol
Stay in the uncle's spare room one more year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses are buying gadgets instead of officers, and the public will pay for it. Every time the city saves money on police, the west side gets fewer of us. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. I'm average at this job and slow on computers, and the force would start counting who uses the new systems best. Officers like me, who police the old way, look bad on a spreadsheet even if the street's quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, and I'd wait to see what's actually forced on us. I'd do the training they make compulsory, but nothing extra. Marisol and I would trim the wedding, maybe skip the hotel reception and do it in the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit insulted, honestly. Like being told the way you were taught is out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies selling this to city hall, and the politicians who want to look modern. Not the officers. Most of us just want to do the job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marisol say about the church hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marisol would say the church hall is where her parents got married, so it's fine. Her mother would want the hotel. Her mother usually wins, but not if the money's not there.

say: Bosses are buying **gadgets instead of officers**, and the public pays.
Every city saving means **fewer of us** on the west side.
think: Being **slow on computers** would make me look bad on a spreadsheet.
The **old way** of policing might quieten a street but won't score well.
do: Do only the **compulsory training** and wait to see what's forced on us.
Move the wedding reception to the **church hall** to save money.
feel: **Worried and insulted**, as if the way he was taught is out of date.
S1.quote: Officers like me, who police the old way, look bad on a spreadsheet even if the street's quieter.
fieldNote: Wei blames **tech companies** and city hall, not colleagues.
He fears being judged by **system use**, not results.
He cuts the wedding before considering any **retraining**.

steps.text: Attend only the compulsory training on new systems
Hold the wedding reception in the church hall
Keep patrolling the west side the same way

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should put the brakes on. You can't hand a city's safety to a machine in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd lose this job within a few years. By 2028 all the forms, the dispatch and the investigations go to AI, and they'd keep the officers who can work with it. By 2031 the robots patrol, and I'm not one of the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wedding forward and keep it tiny, so at least Marisol and I are settled. I'd lean on family: my uncle's room, my dad's contacts at the bus depot, the church noticeboard for work. And I'd cut everything, no car, no eating out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and angry at the same time. Angry at whoever decided this, scared for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward rather than delay it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything's falling apart, I want to be married to my fiancée Marisol before it does. Family is what gets you through. My grandparents married in a bad year and stayed together fifty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots buy you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of doing the walking part while the computer does the thinking. Maybe less pay. I'd use it to find something with my hands, like my dad's trade, but I'm not sure he could get me in.

say: It's **madness**, and someone should put the brakes on.
You can't hand a **city's safety** to a machine in two years.
think: I'd **lose this job** within a few years after 2028.
When robots patrol by 2031, **I'm not kept**.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it tiny.
Lean on **family and church** for a room, contacts and work leads.
Cut **everything**: no car, no eating out.
feel: **Scared and angry**: angry at whoever decided, scared for his family.
S2.quote: If everything's falling apart, I want to be married to my fiancée Marisol before it does.
fieldNote: Wei reaches for **family and faith** before any job market move.
He **brings the wedding forward**, unusually, as an anchor.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Ask Dad's contacts at the bus depot about work
Sell the car and stop eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow it down, and make sure the people in charge answer for what happens. Five years isn't long for a whole city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me until about 2031 before the paperwork side goes, and 2034 before the patrol does. I'd be thirty-five. That's not old, but I'd have a wife and maybe a baby by then, and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad if his old boss at the bus depot takes apprentices in mechanics, and start part-time if they do. Marisol and I would get married as planned and save hard, aiming for two months by 2030. I'd stay in the force while it lasts, because the pay's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but less wild. Five years is enough to learn a trade, if someone gives me the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a mechanic's job also going to robots eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but later than mine, and old buses break in stupid ways. My dad fixed the same engines for thirty years. I'd trust a trade over a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving cities for police work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My family's here, Marisol's family's here, the church is here. I'd rather do a different job in my own neighbourhood than the same job somewhere I don't know anyone.

say: Slow it down and make the **people in charge** answer for what happens.
**Five years** isn't long for a whole city to adjust.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** when patrol goes, with a wife and maybe a baby.
I have **no other trade** to fall back on.
do: Ask Dad about a **mechanic apprenticeship** at the bus depot.
Marry as planned and save toward **two months** by 2030.
Stay in the **force** while the pay lasts.
feel: **Frightened** but less wild; five years is enough to learn a trade.
S3.quote: I'd rather do a different job in my own neighbourhood than the same job somewhere I don't know anyone.
fieldNote: Wei won't **move cities**, even to stay a police officer.
He trusts a **hands-on trade** over anything screen-based.
His father's **depot contacts** are his main route out.

steps.text: Ask Dad's old boss about a part-time mechanic apprenticeship
Save toward two months of expenses by 2030
Hold the church wedding next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people to find their feet, but the government should still keep an eye on these companies. And families should stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right for most of it. I could be a sergeant by 2036 if I keep my nose clean, and sergeants deal with people, not forms. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven with a family and a house, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and go for my sergeant's exam in three years. Marisol and I would marry next summer and start saving for a deposit. I'd only look at a trade if the force started laying people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still a knot in my stomach, because the end's the same, but I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The sergeant's exam has a lot of written work. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I'd ask Sergeant Reyes to help me study. Marisol's good with writing, and she'd help too, though she'd tease me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want them soon after the wedding. Ten years' warning wouldn't change that. If anything, I'd want children before everything changes, so they grow up knowing a normal world for a bit.

say: Ten years is enough for people to **find their feet**.
Government should still **watch these companies**, and families should stick together.
think: I could be a **sergeant by 2036**, dealing with people, not forms.
By 2039 I'd hope for a **family and a house**.
do: Sit the **sergeant's exam** in three years with help from Sergeant Reyes.
Marry next summer and save for a **house deposit**.
Look at a **trade** only if layoffs start.
feel: **Better**, though a knot in the stomach stays.
S4.quote: I'd want children before everything changes, so they grow up knowing a normal world for a bit.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Wei **stay in his lane**: promotion, marriage, children.
He would act only on **real layoffs**, not forecasts.
Children are **brought forward**, not delayed, by the warning.

steps.text: Study for the sergeant's exam with Sergeant Reyes
Marry next summer and save for a house deposit
Plan to have children soon after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time, no other trade, a wedding to pay for. What would help is the government keeping the companies in check, and apprenticeships, real ones, for people my age who need to learn something with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the neighbourhood. My grandmother still lives three streets from the station. If a robot is patrolling my grandma's street, who is she going to call when she's scared at night? That's what I'd want someone in charge to answer.

headlineQuote: If a robot is patrolling my grandma's street, who is she going to call when she's scared at night?
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old patrol officer** working the west side neighbourhood where he grew up.
He's engaged to Marisol, a **teaching assistant**, and rents a room at his uncle's to save.
He distrusts new systems and blames **tech companies** and city hall for cutting officers.
Under fast AGI he'd **marry sooner** and lean on family, church and his father's contacts.
With ten years he'd aim for **sergeant**, start a family and only switch trade if layoffs began.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he has no other trade and a wedding to pay for.
whatWouldHelp: **Real apprenticeships** for young adults and the government keeping AI companies in check.
